sn12.17:1.1: The things that are “made by oneself” and “made by another” are here said to be “suffering” (as at [sn12.24](), [sn12.26]()). Since suffering comes with its opposite, sometimes it is said to be “pleasure and pain” ([an6.95](), [sn12.18](), [sn12.25]()). Since pleasure and pain characterize the world, to that is sometimes added “the self and the cosmos” ([dn29:34.13](), [ud6.5](), [ud6.6]()). To emphasize universality, it can also be all factors of  dependent origination ([sn12.67]()). While these discourses reject the notion since it assumes a metaphysical self, from a conventional point of view it may still be said that good deeds “done by oneself” are a friend in the hereafter ([sn1.53:2.5]()), or that a thief is punished for what they themselves have done ([mil5.3.11:3.7]()); also compare [dhp347](), “like a spider caught in the web she wove”. Later canonical texts, on the other hand, deny that merit is “made by oneself or given by gods” ([ja524:28.2](), [vv84:22.2](), [pv37:22.2]()).
sn12.17:1.4: Naked ascetics are still found in India today. Digambara Jains went naked, but if he were a Jain he would have been introduced as such. Kassapa is an ancient clan name of the brahmins, and we meet four naked ascetics named Kassapa in the canon (here, [dn8](), [sn41.9](), and [mn124]()). They cannot be the same person, for at the end of each account it is said they went forth and attained arahantship.
sn12.17:2.8: This is intensely realistic: whenever someone says to me, “Just a small question”, it’s usually followed by, “So, what is consciousness really? And how does it relate to Nibbana?”
sn12.17:3.1: This draws on the Vedic notion that the act of creation is a kind of self-emptying, as the creator deity forms the world by and of themselves. Thus the sacrificer offers to Prajāpati as the sun with the words, “You are self-made” (_svāṁkṛta_, Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 4.1.1.22, 4.1.2.21). In another context, Atharva Veda 8.5.9c refers to magic spells performed by oneself or prepared by another.
sn12.17:3.3: For Pali _paraṅkata_ we find Sanskrit _anyakṛta_: “Let me not suffer for what was done by another, o king” (Rig Veda 2.28, cf. 6.51.7). Malicious dealings, violence, curses, and maleficent spirits were potent sources of suffering.
sn12.17:3.5: When suffering arises on a personal level, particular instances of suffering might be attributed solely to either oneself or the other. Sometimes it may be both, for example, if someone who acts in compliance with an evil regime is subsequently punished. But if we speak of suffering *in general*, then suffering that is *purely* one’s own fault might occur if all things are determined by one’s own past deeds. And suffering that is *purely* another’s fault might arise from the will of a malevolent deity. Suffering that is both might occur, for example, for one who invokes a malevolent entity to curse another, and then suffers due to their own deed and a counter-curse.
sn12.17:3.7: _Adhicca_ is usually translated in this context as “chance”. The Sanskrit _uddhṛtya_ refers to something that has been “lifted out”, making it a “special exception”. It isn’t used in Sanskrit for a philosophical theory of chance, for which we find instead _yadṛcchā_ (“arbitrariness”, Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.2). The theory proposed here is not that the universe in general operates by chance, but that the happenstance of creation is a “special exception” to the normal workings of causality. Two examples of this belief are given at [dn1:2.30.1]().
sn12.17:3.12: That this is a question is confirmed below at [sn12.17:4.6]().
sn12.17:5.1: See Bodhi’s note on this passage in *Connected Discourses*. | _Pareti_ normally means “to depart”, literally “go to the other”, and its use here is apparently unique. I take it in the sense “convey the meaning”, “imply” (cf. Sanskrit _pārayati_, “convey”).
sn12.17:7.1: Note that, contra BB’s note, pabbajja and upasampada are into the state of a bhikkhu. there’s no mention of a novice. generally, in the early texts, pabbajja and upasampada were synonyms, and there was no separate state of novice or period spent as a novice before ordination. This gradually developed, and makes its way into a few passages.
